channel.title: From the District Attorney — Tripp Fitzner
channel.description: Updates from the Office of the District Attorney, Middle Judicial Circuit of Georgia

item.title: The death penalty in Georgia
item.description:
I see comments from folks on Facebook about the death penalty. Why we didn’t ask for it in a particular case. It’s a fair question, and it deserves a serious answer. First, let me say that there is a checklist of criteria that must be met before you even file a death notice in a case. And it’s binary. You either meet the criteria or you do not. Georgia has 33 people on death row. In the past six years the state has carried out one execution, and none in 2025 or 2026.

A death sentence in Georgia doesn’t end the case. It starts a new one that can run for decades. The Georgia Supreme Court must review every death sentence, and from there it can go to the U.S. Supreme Court. Then comes a new lawsuit in Butts County, where death row is, challenging the conviction and sentence, and from there back up to the Georgia Supreme Court and the U.S. Supreme Court again. Then another new lawsuit in federal court, an appeal to the Eleventh Circuit, sometimes to the full court, and a third trip to the U.S. Supreme Court. When all of that is done comes the execution order, then a clemency hearing before the Parole Board and last-minute suits in state and federal court.

Willie Pye is the one person Georgia has executed in the past six years. The killing was in November 1993. He was sentenced to death in June 1996, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed it in 1998. His lawsuit in Butts County was filed in 2000 and denied in 2012. That’s twelve years in one court on one stage. His federal case was filed in 2013 and denied in 2018. In April 2021 a three-judge panel of the Eleventh Circuit threw out the death sentence. In October 2022 the full Eleventh Circuit reversed that. In October 2023 the U.S. Supreme Court declined to take the case. That’s another ten years in federal court. He was executed on March 20, 2024, 30 years after the crime. Nationally, the people executed in 2023 had spent an average of about 23 years on death row.

In November 2003, two people were killed in Cobb County. The man convicted was sentenced to death in September 2007, and the Georgia Supreme Court affirmed in 2010. His Butts County case ran from 2011 to 2016, and the Georgia Supreme Court refused the appeal in 2017. His federal case ran from 2018 until October 2025, when the U.S. Supreme Court declined it. The execution was set for December 17, 2025. Two days before, the Parole Board suspended it amid a fight over a board member’s conflict of interest, and then a Fulton County judge blocked a new date for months. It was reset for September 16, 2026. The night before, a Cobb County judge stayed it for a hearing under a 2025 Georgia law that lets someone already serving a sentence ask to be resentenced if abuse they suffered was a significant factor in the crime. His lawyer cited childhood abuse. The Georgia Supreme Court left the stay in place and hears argument December 8. That’s nearly 23 years since the crime, 19 since the sentence, and still no end.

For a family, a death sentence doesn’t close anything. It opens decades of waiting on the next ruling, with no say in when it comes or how it turns out.

And once the jury returns a death sentence, those decades are out of our hands. After trial, our office and the Attorney General’s office answer the first appeal together, and from then on the Attorney General represents the State in the lawsuits that follow, in state and federal court. The courts set the pace. What comes back to the district attorney is asking a judge for an execution order when every court is finished, and as that Cobb County case shows, even then the date can be stopped.

I will tell you that I support the death penalty. But as things stand, it is technically legal but practically almost impossible. And during the 25-30 years of endless appeals and court dates the ones who need closure the most are the ones who can’t move on.

item.title: Needed
item.description:
We don’t know which day will be the last one we are needed to tie our child’s shoes. Or teach them how to ride a bike. Or make them look both ways before they cross the street. One day they just do it themselves. As parents we notice, and we know how it feels.

I couldn’t count the number of times I’ve said “You’re old enough to know how to do this” while simultaneously feeling satisfaction that they do not, in fact, know how to do it. They need me to show them. That is how parenting works. Teaching our kids to need us less while being terrified that one day they won't need us at all.

And when something hurts them, or someone does, there’s that pull to fix it. To tell them everything will be okay, whether it will be or not. We want to swoop in and solve their problems while wanting them to be able to solve their own problems.

Being a parent is a bundle of contradictions. Push and pull. Competing objectives dancing on the head of a pin. It’s a wonder any of us get it right. But the joy comes from the same place as the sorrow: the journey, not the destination. So perhaps the point is to raise our kids into people who won’t really need us, but who will show us the grace to make us believe they do.

item.title: Sitting beside them
item.description:
When a kid gets bored there's almost always a cell phone or iPad or something with a screen nearby. Our sons and daughters grow up with plenty of things competing for their attention, and learning to give that attention to something that isn't trying to entertain them takes practice. Taking them deer hunting gives us a chance to sit beside them while they learn.

In a deer stand, there may be a long stretch when nothing much happens. You can't make the woods get interesting on demand. So you help them learn what to watch for and what to listen to. A sound has them looking one way, and a little movement draws their eyes somewhere else. They begin to notice things they would've missed while wishing something would happen. Being quiet and still gives them a chance to see what the world does when nobody's making noise.

That takes some patience, especially when they're tired or their feet are cold, or it's hot and the gnats won't leave their face alone. A mosquito can make being still seem like an unreasonable thing to ask of anybody. We're beside them to help them through those small discomforts, and that takes some patience from us, too.

And after all that, you may walk back without a deer. They paid attention, they stayed quiet, and they tried hard. Nothing came within range. That's a hard part of hunting to explain to a child who wanted so badly to get one, because there isn't anything you can promise about next time, either.

We don't have to talk them out of being disappointed before we reach the truck. But we can help them see that a hunt without a deer wasn't a day when they did everything wrong, or a reason to quit. They learned something they can take back to the stand. And perhaps far beyond it.

That's what I learned from hunting, and what I hope they learn too. Practice being still, paying attention when it isn't easy, and giving something their effort without knowing how it'll turn out. And when they come home empty-handed, going back out again.

item.title: Early voting dates
More tools
item.description:
Buying a man a new set of tools doesn’t necessarily mean he’s going to get rid of the old ones. It means he now has more tools. This is worth understanding before making plans for the extra space in the shed (no wives will be named or shamed in this post).

His reasoning is usually pretty sound. There’s nothing wrong with the old tools. For example, the wrench. The new set came with one the same size, but that’s hardly the old wrench’s fault is it? And sometimes you need one wrench to hold something while you turn it with the other. Throwing one away would leave you buying a third wrench to replace the first one, which he’d have a hard time explaining to himself.

The saw is dull. He’ll grant you that. But a dull saw is still a saw, and he’s been meaning to get it sharpened for going on eleven years. But the circular saw is just so convenient. Still he's certain the day will come when he'll need that old hand saw in easy reach.

The hammer handle has been taped so many times it's more tape than wood. But it has a balance the new one doesn’t have, and he knows exactly where it’s going to hit. The new one will have to prove itself, just like the old one did.

Then there’s the coffee can. Nobody knows everything that’s in it, including him. Bolts, washers, a hinge pin, a spring off of something. None of it matches, and every piece of it will be needed about a week after the can goes to the dump. (Every man knows the bolts and bits you need are the ones you threw away).

Some of those tools were his daddy’s, and a few were his granddaddy’s before that. Back when tools were built to last and fathers taught their sons how to hammer straight, measure twice, and cut true. The tools aren't just tools. They are a door into memory.

Here's what I can promise. In his heart, he's hoping one day his son will stand where he is standing, looking at the old tools he passed on. Deciding what to keep, and understanding that new isn't always better. Because while you can always have more tools, you can't always make more memories with the ones who taught you to use them.

item.title: When someone tells you what's happening at home
item.description:
October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month, and part of prevention is knowing how to respond when someone tells you what's happening at home.

Listen without blaming them or asking why they've stayed. Leaving an abusive relationship can be difficult and dangerous. What may look simple to you...isn't. It never is. For the victim, it involves fears and risks you don't know and they likely can't fully explain. The point of domestic violence isn't really violence. It's control. And the person committing the abuse is responsible for it, not the person trying to get through it.

Domestic violence often isolates people from the very ones who could help them. If you're worried about someone, stay in touch in a way that's safe for them. Ask what they need rather than deciding for them. Offer to help them talk with an advocate about their options and a safety plan. Keep offering support even if they stay or return.

If you or someone you know is in an abusive relationship, Georgia's domestic violence hotline is 1-800-33-HAVEN, or 1-800-334-2836. You can call if you need to talk. If you're in immediate danger, call 911.

item.title: A new home for the office online
item.description:
This office has rebuilt its website. The address and phone number are current, the biography is current, and two things are new.

First, the office's closed-case numbers are now published on The Record. Closed cases are public record, and the people of this circuit are entitled to see what their District Attorney's office does with its docket.

Second, the documents people actually ask for are gathered in one place: the office's Use of Force Protocol, the Early Intervention Program guide and forms, and record restriction paperwork, all on Files & Policies. Open records requests go to Investigator Rocky Davis, and his contact information is on the Contact page.

Updates from the office will post here.
